# Dates: types, parts, truncation

Dates are real types in SQL. A DATE holds a day, such as `DATE '2025-03-15'`. A TIMESTAMP holds a day and a time, such as `TIMESTAMP '2025-03-15 23:30:00'`. Store dates as dates, not as text: then you can compare them, cut them into periods and take their parts.

## Truncate to group by a period

`date_trunc('month', order_ts)` cuts a time back to the start of its month: any time in March 2025 becomes 2025-03-01. When a question asks for the first day of a period as a date, a date or a midnight timestamp both pass. Other units are `'year'`, `'quarter'`, `'week'` and `'day'`. Group by the truncated value to get one row per period. The year stays in it, so March 2024 and March 2025 stay apart.

`GROUP BY 1` groups by the first column of the SELECT list, so you need not repeat a long date expression.

## Take a part of a date

`year(d)`, `quarter(d)`, `month(d)`, `hour(ts)` and `dayname(d)` each take one part. `EXTRACT(month FROM d)` is the standard spelling, and `date_part('month', d)` works too. A part on its own loses the rest of the date: `month(d)` gives 3 for March of every year. Group by the month number only within one year, or keep the year beside it.

## ISO weeks

An ISO week starts on Monday, and week 1 is the week with the year's first Thursday. So 29, 30 and 31 December 2025 are in week 1 of 2026. `week(d)` gives the ISO week number and `isoyear(d)` the year that week belongs to. Pair the week with `isoyear`, never with `year`. `date_trunc('week', d)` gives the Monday that starts the week.

Weekday numbers differ: `isodow(d)` counts Monday as 1 and Sunday as 7, while `dayofweek(d)` counts Sunday as 0.

## Times are stored in UTC

Every `_ts` column, such as `orders.order_ts` and `competitor_prices.observed_ts`, holds the moment in UTC. Amsterdam is 1 hour ahead of UTC in winter and 2 hours in summer, so an order at 23:30 UTC is already the next day in Amsterdam. When a question asks for an Amsterdam day, week, month or hour, convert first:

```sql
timezone('Europe/Amsterdam', timezone('UTC', order_ts))
```

The inner call marks the stored time as UTC; the outer one gives the Amsterdam clock time for that moment. Then take the date with a CAST, or truncate it. A single `order_ts AT TIME ZONE 'Europe/Amsterdam'` is not enough: it reads the stored time as Amsterdam time and moves it the wrong way. The `order_date`, `order_week` and `order_month` columns of `sales` are UTC days.

## Ranges on times

On a TIMESTAMP, an end date means midnight at its start. For all of 2025, keep `order_ts >= TIMESTAMP '2025-01-01 00:00:00'` and `order_ts < TIMESTAMP '2026-01-01 00:00:00'`.

## How to answer a date question

1. Find the clock: UTC, or Amsterdam time. Convert first if it is Amsterdam.
2. Find the period: a day, ISO week, month, quarter or year, or a part such as the weekday.
3. Truncate to group by periods; take a part when the question wants a number or a name.
4. Filter with a range that keeps every moment of the first and last day.
syntax_md:
```sql
SELECT date_trunc('month', order_ts) AS order_month,   -- metrics: the start of each month, year kept
       COUNT(*) AS orders                             -- metrics: one count per month
FROM orders                                           -- source and grain: one row per order
WHERE order_ts >= TIMESTAMP '2025-01-01 00:00:00'     -- row filter: every moment of 2025
  AND order_ts < TIMESTAMP '2026-01-01 00:00:00'
GROUP BY 1;                                           -- one row per month
```

- Truncate: `date_trunc('day' | 'week' | 'month' | 'quarter' | 'year', d)`. Weeks start on Monday.
- Parts: `year(d)`, `quarter(d)`, `month(d)`, `week(d)` (ISO), `isoyear(d)`, `isodow(d)` (Monday 1 to Sunday 7), `dayofweek(d)` (Sunday 0), `hour(ts)`, `dayname(d)`. Portable: `EXTRACT(month FROM d)`.
- Literals: `DATE '2025-06-30'`, `TIMESTAMP '2025-06-30 23:30:00'`.
- Amsterdam time from a UTC column: `timezone('Europe/Amsterdam', timezone('UTC', order_ts))`, then `CAST(... AS DATE)` for the Amsterdam day.
- A day from a timestamp: `CAST(order_ts AS DATE)`.
dialect_note: In DuckDB 1.5, date_trunc on a DATE returns a TIMESTAMP: date_trunc('month', DATE '2025-03-15') gives 2025-03-01 00:00:00. CAST it to DATE when you want to show a date; the grader treats a DATE and a TIMESTAMP as the same kind of value, so either passes. date_trunc('month', d) has the same argument order in PostgreSQL, while SQLite uses date(d, 'start of month'). date_trunc('week', d) starts weeks on Monday, as ISO weeks do: week(d) is the ISO week number and isoyear(d) its year. Weekday numbers differ by engine: DuckDB's dayofweek counts Sunday as 0 and isodow counts Monday as 1 and Sunday as 7; PostgreSQL's dow counts Sunday as 0, and BigQuery's DAYOFWEEK runs from 1 for Sunday to 7. BigQuery's WEEK begins on Sunday and its ISOWEEK on Monday. Every _ts column in this course holds UTC time, so convert it before you take an Amsterdam day.

worked_examples.title: Web orders per calendar month
worked_examples.prompt: How many web orders did Voltmarkt take in each calendar month of 2025? Use the orders table and keep the orders with channel 'web'. order_ts holds the time in UTC, so take the month in UTC. Return order_month, the first day of the month, and orders, one row for each month.

clauses.why: date_trunc cuts each order time back to the first day of its month and keeps the year.
COUNT(*) counts every web order in the month, guest orders included.
orders has one row per order, so each row counted is one order.
Up to but not including the first moment of 2026, so the whole of 31 December stays in.
One row per month: the same expression as in SELECT.

worked_examples.title: Web orders per Amsterdam day
worked_examples.prompt: How many web orders did Voltmarkt take on each Amsterdam calendar day from 2025-10-24 to 2025-10-27? order_ts holds the time in UTC. Return order_day, the Amsterdam date, and orders, one row for each day.

clauses.text: SELECT CAST(timezone('Europe/Amsterdam', timezone('UTC', order_ts)) AS DATE) AS order_day,
clauses.why: Mark the stored time as UTC, turn it into Amsterdam clock time, then keep the date.
One count for each Amsterdam day.

clauses.text: AND CAST(timezone('Europe/Amsterdam', timezone('UTC', order_ts)) AS DATE) BETWEEN DATE '2025-10-24' AND DATE '2025-10-27'
clauses.why: Pick the days by their Amsterdam date too, so both ends of the range are Amsterdam midnights; the clock change on 26 October needs no extra care.
One row per Amsterdam day: GROUP BY 1 groups by the first column of the SELECT list.

why_clause.clause: CAST(timezone('Europe/Amsterdam', timezone('UTC', order_ts)) AS DATE) AS order_day
why_clause.stem: Why is order_ts wrapped in two timezone calls before the CAST to DATE?

options.text: The inner call marks the stored time as UTC, and the outer one gives the Amsterdam clock time for that moment.
The two calls cancel each other out, so the date stays the UTC day.
One call would also work; the second only makes the query portable.
The inner call rounds the time to the hour, and the outer one removes the time of day.

why_clause.explanation: order_ts holds a UTC moment with no time zone attached. timezone('UTC', order_ts) says which moment that is, and timezone('Europe/Amsterdam', ...) shows that moment on an Amsterdam clock, 1 or 2 hours later. Only then does the CAST take the Amsterdam date. A single AT TIME ZONE 'Europe/Amsterdam' reads the stored time as Amsterdam time and moves it the wrong way.
